item.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
item.abstract: We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point. When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything. It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating. The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists. Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives. Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem. Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge. We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one. We split the system into two layers: The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request: Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded. One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space: Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability. Each subagent follows a standardized structure: This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first. Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent. Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour. For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists. The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems. The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries: This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit: The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained. We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes. The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable. This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include: Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin. The post The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do appeared first on Engineering at Meta .

item.title: MiniMax Just Launched M3.1 Flash: 428B MoE Agentic Model at $0.15/M Input
item.abstract: MiniMax has just released MiniMax M3.1 Flash on its API, priced at $0.15 per 1M input tokens . MiniMax also confirmed that Space Bunny was an earlier M3.1 Flash build. That stealth model processed over 200T tokens. For developers, the message is near-frontier agentic scores at Flash-tier cost. Model weights are due in late October, 2026. MiniMax M3.1 Flash is a multimodal mixture-of-experts model from MiniMax. It targets coding, agentic office work and visual reasoning. MiniMax’s product page lists 428B total parameters and about 23B active. It also mentions sparse attention and a native visual encoder. The model accepts text, image and video input and returns text. The context window is 1,000,000 tokens. Those parameter totals match MiniMax M3 , which ships at ~428B total and ~23B active. MiniMax has not published a technical report on what changed in the Flash variant. Reasoning is always on and cannot be disabled. Developers choose from 5 effort levels: Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max. MiniMax recommends Max as the default. Migration matters here. Requests sending thinking.type=disabled or effort=none return an error. Reasoning arrives in a separate reasoning_content field, which may be absent. Integrations that parse inline <think> tags from M3 need updating. All scores below are MiniMax-reported. No independent replication exists yet. On the CoWork set, M3.1 Flash leads Automation-Bench v1.0.6 at 62.2 . Opus 5 scores 50.3 and GPT-5.6 Sol 45.8. It ties Opus 5 on BankerToolBench at 76.2. It also tops LOCA-Bench 256K at 60.3. Agents’ Last Exam lands at 29.6. Coding results are mixed. DeepSWE v1.1 scores 73.7, just above GPT-5.6 Sol at 73.0. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 scores higher at 77.0. Terminal Bench 4.0 is the weakest result at 38.1. SWE Refactor Bench sits at 23.0, versus 31.0 for Opus 5. On vision, BabyVision with tools reaches 91.0 and CharXiv RQ reaches 82.5. HLE without tools scores 43.4. Spot checks hold up. The Kimi K3 model card reports DeepSWE 67.5 and BabyVision 85.7, matching MiniMax’s table. One inconsistency: MiniMax’s cost chart plots Automation-Bench max effort at 62.8, while its table says 62.2. MiniMax frames value as cost per task, not per token. On its Automation-Bench chart, all 5 effort levels sit below $0.05 per task. Scores range from 52.8 at low effort to 62.8 at max. A full 152-task Agents’ Last Exam run cost about $111 at 29.6. On DeepSWE, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash-1017 plots both higher and cheaper at max effort. The model is live on platform.minimax.io as MiniMax-M3.1-Flash . MiniMax supports Anthropic-compatible and OpenAI-compatible access, including Chat Completions and Responses. It is also available through M Plan and the MiniMax Code desktop app . Pricing is a flat $0.15 input and $0.60 output per 1M tokens. Cache reads cost $0.015 per 1M. There is no long-context surcharge. MiniMax M3 costs $0.30/$1.20 up to 512K input and doubles above that. Per token, Flash is half of M3’s standard rate. MiniMax claims 1/3 the cost of M3 but has not detailed the calculation. On speed, MiniMax’s product page lists about 150 tokens per second. The announcement claims 3x the speed of M3. Weights arrive October 23; the license is not yet disclosed. For scale, M3’s MXFP8 build is about 440 GB . *Scores from MiniMax’s comparison table . Kimi K3 DeepSWE and BabyVision match its own card. Every benchmark is vendor-reported, and harness choice shifts results. Automation-Bench numbers do not transfer across sources. Kimi K3’s card reports 30.8 on a 600-task public subset, while MiniMax lists 46.7. Opus 5 leads by 13.7 points on Terminal Bench 4.0 and 14.1 on NL2Repo-Bench. Always-on reasoning also sets a token and latency floor for simple calls. Self-hosting details remain unknown until October 23. Check out the announcement , product page and API docs . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter . item.title: Improve TTFT for multi-turn agentic workloads with bi-directional KV transfer in vLLM
item.abstract: Multi-turn agentic workloads build on accumulated context as an agent reasons, invokes tools, and incorporates earlier results. With each new turn, the client resends the conversation history, including system instructions, prior prompts, tool results, and model responses, causing the growing context to be processed repeatedly. In Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation , each request is split across specialized nodes: the prefill node processes the prompt and builds its key-value (KV) cache, then the decode node retrieves those KV blocks and generates the response. Conventional disaggregated serving, however, only transfers KV cache in one direction: from prefill to decode node. This one-directional flow creates two inefficiencies for multi-turn workloads. First, after generating a response, the decode node holds KV cache entries for both the prompt and the newly generated tokens. When processing the next turn, the prefill node cannot retrieve those entries, so it must recompute the KV projections for the previous response tokens. Second, the decode node maintains the session state while the prefill nodes don’t, increasing the probability of cache eviction for active sessions on the prefill nodes. On a full cache miss, the prefill node must recompute KV projections for the entire conversation history, including system instructions, prior user requests, tool results, and model-generated responses. As the conversation grows, this redundant work consumes more accelerator capacity and increases time to first token (TTFT). When you build conversational assistants and agentic applications, longer interaction histories can increase latency and consume accelerator capacity through repeated prefill computation. In this post, we show how bi-directional KV cache transfer lets prefill and decode nodes reuse previously computed context across turns, which improves accelerator utilization and helps applications sustain responsive TTFT as conversations grow. In our multi-turn benchmarks on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances, bi-directional KV transfer reduced TTFT by up to 1.6x for Qwen3-32B and up to 3.3x for zai-org/GLM-5-FP8 (see the Performance data section). Results vary with workload and configuration. The instances are connected with AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA ), a low-latency remote direct memory access (RDMA) network used across servers in AWS. On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory on the prefill and decode nodes. We originally built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA and contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic capability. The results presented here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en GPU cluster with EFA, showing that the benefits also carry over to GPUs. This post explains the bi-directional KV transfer architecture, router metadata flow, KV-block retention and recompute controls, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. Bi-directional KV transfer is a mechanism in which a decode node returns previously computed KV to a prefill node on subsequent turns of a conversation. This avoids recomputing shared context on the prefill node and is governed by a configurable KV recompute threshold. It mitigates both computational-redundancy scenarios described earlier. To make it work, the KV must survive past the turn that produced it and travel in the reverse direction, coordinated by a KV-cache-aware router. We extended the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) KV connector to let prefill nodes consume remote KV blocks, similar to how decode nodes already consume KV blocks that the prefill node provides. This is not a trivial change, because the two node types are architecturally different: prefill nodes compute KV representations for new prompt tokens and can provide complete prompt KV blocks. Decode nodes lack the capability (or efficiency) to generate complete KV representations and can only serve previously cached KV blocks. As a result, prefill and decode nodes still carry their own roles and logic for computing the metadata of remote and local KV blocks. The actual KV transfer mechanism (a NIXL READ), however, is common to both the P->D and D->P directions. The following diagram first shows the existing flow in blue. The router sends the request to prefill node, prefill node computes the prompt KV and returns its block metadata, and the router forwards the request and metadata to decode node for the standard P→D NIXL READ. The numbered red path illustrates the bi-directional KV transfer additions: (1) decode node retains eligible KV blocks after generation, (2) returns their metadata in the streaming response, and (3) the router caches that metadata for the next prefill request. Prefill node then (4) checks the remotely reusable KV after it applies local cache matches, (5) queues an asynchronous receive when the reusable token count meets the threshold, and (6) performs a D→P NIXL READ before computing the remaining suffix. Figure 1: Standard prefill-to-decode flow (blue) and the bi-directional KV transfer additions (red) vLLM includes connector-side support for bi-directional KV transfer, while coordinating KV reuse across conversation turns requires a KV-cache-aware router. vLLM GitHub provides an example proxy that implements the flow used in this post which can be adapted for your environment. The KV-cache-aware router is a lightweight, stateful control-plane component between the client, prefill, and decode nodes. It maintains an in-memory mapping from the client-provided conversation_id to decode’s kv_transfer_params . The router stores only block-location metadata, not KV tensors, and obtains that metadata from the response stream rather than separately querying decode node. The following diagram shows how the router manages KV metadata across conversation turns. On the first turn, the cache lookup misses and the request follows the standard P→D flow. The router then saves decode’s metadata from the response stream. On later turns, the router retrieves that metadata using the conversation_id so prefill can reuse KV from decode. It then refreshes the metadata after generation for the next turn. Figure 2: KV-cache-aware router metadata flow across conversation turns Normally a decode instance frees a request’s blocks as soon as generation finishes. Under bi-directional KV transfer mode, it holds them for a configurable lifetime ( decoder_kv_blocks_ttl , default 480 seconds) and publishes their location and expiry. The conversation’s KV, both prompt prefix and generated response, then stays available for the next turn. For a turn that arrives before the time to live (TTL) expires, prefill node reuses the KV. One that arrives later falls back to normal prefill. Because this TTL is fixed and not renewed, tune it to the expected time between turns to balance KV reuse against accelerator-memory usage. A natural next improvement is to extend the heartbeat-renewed lease to the decode side. A decode instance could then reclaim blocks as soon as a conversation goes idle rather than at the end of a fixed timer. KV reuse isn’t always faster than local recomputation. For a short reusable prefix, interconnect and coordination overhead can exceed the time needed to recompute the tokens. The kv_recompute_threshold setting, which defaults to 64 tokens, controls this decision. Prefill node recomputes when the token count to compute is below the threshold and pulls KV from decode node when it is at or above the threshold. Deployments can tune this value based on model computation time, KV size, and interconnect performance. For evaluation, we used Qwen3-32B and GLM-5-FP8 models on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon EC2 P5en instances connected with EFA.

item.title: Nvidia launches new open models to run agents in the enterprise and on PCs
item.abstract: Nvidia on Thursday launched new open-weight models designed for always-on agents and edge computing. The Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is a large, 120-billion-parameter model geared for agents used by the enterprise. While it uses fewer parameters than the Nemotron 3 Ultra model, Nvidia says it can deliver similar accuracy in instruction-following and tool-use tasks. At the other end of the spectrum, the company also launched two lightweight Bolt models. These are intended to run locally on the new AI PCs (running the Nvidia RTX Spark chip) and workstations running the DGX Spark. Such PCs, aimed at consumers, programmers, and enterprise knowledge workers, are being released right now into the market through partners like Microsoft and Dell. “Any organization that wants to run agents on Nvidia infrastructure now has an open, optimized model for their tier without having to choose between capability and deployability,” Nvidia’s vice president of Open Models and Software, Kari Briski, wrote in the blog post announcing these models. Nvidia claims that the Super VL completes tasks faster than competing models from Anthropic and OpenAI (Opus 5, GPT 6.1 Sol, Luna, Astra) when post-trained on specific agentic tasks. These tasks include document intelligence, financial accounting, scientific experimentation, medical insurance claims, and security attack resilience. While such claims are standard whenever a major tech company announces a new model, Nvidia has backed it up with a list of heavy-hitter companies that it says are using Super VL. These include Skydance, EY, Ramp, Crowdstrike, Perplexity, and Salesforce . Of course, these aren’t the first open-weight models that Nvidia has released that compete with the proprietary frontier labs — companies that are both its customers and its investments. The GPU giant has an entire family of Nemotron models that do everything from multimodal artificial intelligence to reasoning, coding, math, and enterprise automation. However, those fast-growing proprietary AI labs are now looking to many other chips and AI system makers beyond Nvidia to power their needs, like AWS’s Trainium and Cerebras, as well as building their own home-grown chips. So Nvidia is leaning hard into the trend of enterprise companies wanting to run their own open models in their own data centers. “Unlike closed frontier models, organizations can post-train Super VL on their own data, deploy it on their own infrastructure and own what they build,” Briski wrote. But with the announcement or the smaller, local PC models, it is also trying to push forward the nascent trend of consumer AI assistants. While it seems a new AI assistant is introduced every day by startups and Big Tech alike, privacy-weary consumers may not want to invite such agents so deeply into their lives giving them access to info about their families, health, finances, and so on. So, while Nvidia hopes to create a new market for itself selling PCs powered by its chips by creating machines that run the models and agents locally, PC users “can delegate everyday projects … without sending those workloads to the cloud,” Briski wrote. Of the two Bolt models, Nemotron 3.5 Bolt 74B-A9B 24GB is a 74-billion parameter model designed for local agentic tasks. It is intended to balance speed with reasoning to handle multistep reasoning, tool calling, and web browsing. The smallest Bolt E4B is aimed at conversational agents. Super VL and Bolt 74B-A9B are available now, with Bolt E4B coming later this month, Nvidia says.

item.title: Claude Haiku 5.5: What’s New and How to Use It for Fast, Cheap AI Workflows
item.abstract: Claude Haiku 5.5: What’s New and How to Use It for Fast, Cheap AI Workflows Claude Haiku 5.5 cuts list prices by 90% and adds adaptive thinking and a 1M token context window. Learn what broke from Haiku 4.5, and build classification, extraction, and sub-agent workflows in Python using the new API. By Shittu Olumide , Technical Content Specialist on October 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence Anthropic released Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7, 2026, and calls it its cheapest, fastest, and most capable small model. The API model ID is claude-haiku-5-5 , and prompts up to 100,000 tokens cost \$0.10 per million input tokens and \$0.50 per million output tokens. This article covers what changed since Haiku 4.5, how to build fast, cheap AI workflows with it in Python (classification, extraction, and sub-agents), and when a bigger Claude model is still the better pick. Haiku 5.5 Anthropic positions Haiku 5.5 for high-volume, cost-sensitive work such as summaries, compaction, database queries, and classification, and as a subagent alongside Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5. It is available on the Claude Platform, Amazon Web Services , Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Its safety evaluations are documented in the system card . Anthropic's deprecation page lists the earliest retirement date as October 7, 2027. What's New Compared With Haiku 4.5? Feature Haiku 4.5 Haiku 5.5 Context window 200K tokens 1M tokens Max output 64K tokens 128K tokens Thinking control Manual thinking budget Adaptive thinking with an effort setting, a first for a Haiku Price per million tokens, prompts up to 100K (input / output) \$1.00 / \$5.00 \$0.10 / \$0.50 Price over 100K \$1.00 / \$5.00 \$0.50 / \$2.50 Smallest cacheable prompt 4,096 tokens 512 tokens GDPval-AA (knowledge work) 735 1620 OSWorld 2.1, offline subset (computer use) 15.7% 72.4% Humanity's Last Exam, no tools 10.2% 45.9% Terminal-Bench 4.0 (agentic coding) 0.0% 39.2% The benchmark rows are Anthropic's own results, and the launch page shows Sonnet 5.5 ahead on all four (for example, 70.6% on Terminal-Bench 4.0). The price cut is also smaller in practice than the list prices suggest. Haiku 5.5 uses a newer tokenizer, so the same text counts as roughly 30% more tokens . Anthropic puts the average saving at around 75% , after accounting for the tokenizer and for the 10% of requests that run over 100K tokens. Three changes can break existing Haiku 4.5 code. The what's-new page lists them as breaking: sending temperature , top_p , or top_k returns an error, ending the messages with an assistant prefill returns an error, and manual thinking with budget_tokens returns an error. Two behavior changes matter as well. Adaptive thinking is on by default, so a response can start with a thinking block, and thinking tokens count toward max_tokens . Safety classifiers can also decline a request, so your code must handle stop_reason: "refusal" . On safety, Anthropic says Haiku 5.5's cybersecurity safeguards are stricter than Haiku 4.5's and block penetration testing. Using Haiku 5.5 for Fast, Cheap Workflows You need Python 3.10 or newer, an API key from the Claude Console, and a recent Anthropic SDK, since the code below uses the newer output_config parameter. pip install -U anthropic export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here" The first command installs or upgrades the official Python SDK. The second stores your key in the shell session, and the SDK reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY automatically. On Windows PowerShell, use $env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="your-key-here" . Step 1: Classification and Extraction These are the two jobs Haiku was built for: a short input and a short, structured answer, repeated thousands of times. The code uses JSON outputs, which constrain the reply to a schema you provide. It also holds the shared price table and a cost helper that the next two scripts reuse. # haiku_tasks.py """Fast, cheap Claude Haiku 5.5 calls: classification and extraction with JSON outputs.""" import json import anthropic MODEL = "claude-haiku-5-5" client = anthropic.Anthropic() # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment # USD per million tokens (input, output) for prompts up to 100K tokens. PRICES = { "claude-haiku-5-5": (0.10, 0.50), "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00), "claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00), } CATEGORY_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "properties": {"category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "shipping", "technical", "other"]}}, "required": ["category"], "additionalProperties": False, } INVOICE_SCHEMA = { "type": "object", "properties": { "vendor": {"type": "string"}, "invoice_number": {"type": "string"}, "total": {"type": "number"}, "currency": {"type": "string"}, "due_date": {"type": "string", "description": "ISO date, YYYY-MM-DD"}, }, "required": ["vendor", "invoice_number", "total", "currency", "due_date"], "additionalProperties": False, } def cost_usd(model, usage): price_in, price_out = PRICES[model] return (usage.input_tokens * price_in + usage.output_tokens * price_out) / 1_000_000 def ask_json(schema, instruction, text, model=MODEL, effort="low"): """One request whose reply must be JSON matching `schema`. Returns (data, usage).""" reply = client.messages.create( model=model, max_tokens=1000, # thinking tokens count toward this limit, so leave headroom system=instruction, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": text}], output_config={"effort": effort, "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": schema}}, ) if reply.stop_reason in ("refusal", "max_tokens"): raise RuntimeError(f"No usable answer, stop reason: {reply.stop_reason}") # A reply can start with a thinking block, so pick the text block by type. answer = "".join(block.text for block in reply.content if block.type == "text") return json.loads(answer), reply.usage def classify(text, model=MODEL): data, usage = ask_json(CATEGORY_SCHEMA, "Classify the customer message.", text, model) return data["category"], usage def extract_invoice(text, model=MODEL): data, usage = ask_json(INVOICE_SCHEMA, "Extract the invoice fields from the text.", text, model) return data, usage if __name__ == "__main__": for message in ["I was charged twice this month.", "My parcel never arrived.", "The app crashes on login."]: category, usage = classify(message) print(f"{category:<10} {usage.input_tokens} in / {usage.output_tokens} out <- {message}") invoice = "Acme Cloud Ltd, invoice AC-2291. Total due: 1,240.50 USD by 15 November 2026." fields, usage = extract_invoice(invoice) print(fields, f"(${cost_usd(MODEL, usage):.6f})") PRICES lists input and output prices per million tokens for the three models (from Anthropic's launch page and pricing page ), and cost_usd turns a response's token counts into dollars. The two schemas describe the output you want: CATEGORY_SCHEMA limits category to four allowed values, and INVOICE_SCHEMA lists five fields. ask_json is the core function. It sends one request with the schema inside output_config.format , and effort set to low , so the model spends little time thinking on an easy task. Anthropic's JSON outputs guarantee valid JSON that matches the schema. Notice what is missing: there is no temperature , because Haiku 5.5 rejects it. max_tokens is 1000 even though answers are tiny, since thinking tokens count against it. Two checks follow. A stop reason of refusal or max_tokens raises an error instead of failing silently on a half-empty reply. Then the text is read by block type, because a reply may begin with a thinking block, and parsed as JSON. I used JSON outputs instead of forcing a tool call on purpose. Haiku 5.5 accepts a forced tool call , but Opus 5.5 rejects one with a 400 error , so JSON outputs are the portable choice for the three-model comparison in Step 3. One caveat: JSON outputs are not available on Amazon Bedrock for Haiku 5.5, so on Bedrock you describe the format in the prompt and validate the result yourself. Run it: python haiku_tasks.

item.title: How Deepgram optimized voice AI at scale with AWS Trainium
item.abstract: As voice becomes a first-class modality for AI, Deepgram’s models span speech-to-text, text-to-speech, and voice agents. They now process quadrillions of audio tokens a year for more than 200,000 developers and 1,400 organizations. Customers use them through the Deepgram API or run them in their own environments, including on Amazon SageMaker AI. For Deepgram, serving efficiency determines how much audio the system can process for a given infrastructure budget. High-volume batch workloads put heavy pressure on that budget, so the more efficiently each accelerator hour is used, the more audio Deepgram can serve on the same fleet. That made inference efficiency a natural target and Deepgram turned to AWS AI chips to improve it. They worked with AWS to bring its Nova-3 speech-to-text model to AWS Trainium2 for offline batch workloads such as contact-center analytics and medical transcription. The engagement began with Deepgram delivering Nova-3 as standard PyTorch code. Over several months, Deepgram and the AWS Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) team ported Nova-3 to AWS Trainium2 in PyTorch reconstruction and tuned it for the new hardware. The final configuration runs eight model replicas on a single Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) trn2.3xlarge instance. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, that setup processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. We measured this using instance pricing at the time of the evaluation. These gains help Deepgram scale efficiently, keep shipping better models, and bring them to customers at lower prices. These benefits can extend to customers who self-host Deepgram models in their own virtual private cloud (VPC) on Amazon SageMaker AI. There, Deepgram and AWS continue to improve ease of setup, reliability, and observability. In this post, we walk through the full inference optimization effort on Trainium: porting Nova-3 to the AWS Neuron software stack, the kernel-level tuning that followed, the data-parallel Rust runtime that lets Deepgram’s own model server call Trainium, and the throughput and cost results we measured on batch transcription. Starting with standard PyTorch code, we used TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch integration of the Neuron Compiler, which supports both eager execution and torch.compile . We ran Nova-3 in eager mode on Trainium2 first and checked which operations fell back to the CPU, then compiled with torch.compile . The compiled path ran every model operation on Trainium2 with no CPU fallbacks detected. We compiled the encoder and decoder as separate static-shape graphs using torch.compile . Throughout, we checked numerical accuracy at two levels: layer-level output consistency against CPU, and the end-to-end Word Error Rate (WER), which had to stay in line with Deepgram’s reference values and target. From that working baseline, we kicked off the optimization work by replacing several layers with fused kernels from the public NKI Library (NKILib), a collection of pre-built reference kernels written with the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI). The kernels covered operations such as fused QKV projections, fused feed-forward network (FFN) layers, and depthwise 1D convolution. We optimized for throughput and, by extension, cost efficiency, targeting Deepgram’s offline inference workloads. Throughput is reported as a relative gain over a baseline configuration rather than as absolute audio processed per second, and we swept batch sizes 1–128 to find the throughput-maximizing batch size. Enabling kernels is only the first step of an optimization flywheel: enable an NKI kernel (custom or from NKILib), profile the workload, then either tune the existing kernel or replace it with a new one based on the profiling insights. This cycle repeats until the performance target is met. At each step, a different part of the Neuron stack accelerates the work: NKILib provides drop-in replacement kernels, Neuron Explorer is the go-to tool for profiling Neuron workloads, and the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) toolkit speeds up profiling analysis and kernel tuning through its profiling and kernel-writing skills. In our case, the NKILib kernels got us most of the way, and profiling showed where a hand-written kernel would do better. Each time, the NAD profiling skills took us from a Neuron Explorer profile to a root cause, and the NAD kernel-writing skills helped produce the replacement kernels. Each Trainium2 device features eight physical NeuronCores, exposed by default as four logical NeuronCores (LNC2). Because each Nova-3 model instance fits comfortably on a single physical core, we reduced the number of physical cores per logical core to one (LNC1). This configuration lets us host eight model replicas (DP8) per Trainium2 device. Inputs are processed concurrently while maximizing per-device throughput. The data-parallel runtime is driven by a work-stealing queue with one thread per replica. Deepgram’s production serving stack is written in Rust, so porting Nova-3 to Trainium2 required more than compiling the model: it also had to run without Python or PyTorch in the serving path. We therefore built a lightweight runtime in which Rust coordinates model replicas through a shared work-stealing queue. A C layer loads and executes ahead-of-time-compiled Neuron Executable File Format (NEFFs) directly through the Neuron Runtime API ( libnrt ). The runtime integrates directly with Deepgram’s serving architecture and reproduced the reference token sequences exactly at every tested batch size. We benchmarked it against multithreaded (MT) and multiprocessing (MP) Python data-parallel runtimes. Compared with the MP baseline, the Rust runtime removes the overhead of the Python interpreter entirely. Compared with the MT baseline, it further alleviates global interpreter lock (GIL) serialization, so dispatch calls from concurrent worker threads are no longer contended within a single process. These gains matter because Nova-3 performs a sequence of small decoder calls for each audio chunk, making host-side dispatch the bottleneck at low batch sizes. The throughput improvement is therefore largest there, and remains meaningful even at the throughput-maximizing batch size. There, the Rust runtime delivered a 7.5% throughput gain over the multiprocessing Python baseline. Figure 1: Deepgram Nova-3 on AWS Trainium2, compiled ahead of time and served from Rust We measured price-performance as audio processed per dollar. On Deepgram’s offline, throughput-oriented batch workloads, the single-device Trainium2 setup (trn2.3xlarge) processed 11–70 percent more audio per dollar than the compute options Deepgram had been running. In this post, we demonstrated how Deepgram and the AWS FDE ported the Nova-3 speech-to-text PyTorch model to Trainium hardware using TorchNeuron, which provides native PyTorch framework integration for AWS Trainium. We improved performance by replacing layers directly with pre-built kernels from NKILib. We then assessed performance using Neuron Explorer and used the Neuron Agentic Development (NAD) profiling skills to query profiling data and accelerate performance troubleshooting. Building on these insights, we adapted kernel source code using the NAD kernel-writing skills. Finally, we built a lightweight Rust data-parallel runtime for AWS Trainium, calling the Neuron Runtime API from Rust. Our setup demonstrated cost savings in offline, throughput-oriented scenarios, validating AWS Trainium as a viable and efficient option for Deepgram’s inference workloads. To try this approach on your own models, start with the AWS Neuron documentation , which covers the compiler, the runtime, and the supported frameworks. The Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) guide explains how to write the kernels described in this post, and the NKI samples repository holds the reference kernels we started from.

item.title: NVIDIA Open Sources Run:ai Under Apache 2.0 for Kubernetes GPU Orchestration
item.abstract: NVIDIA has released the full NVIDIA Run:ai platform as open source software. The source code ships under the Apache 2.0 license on GitHub. NVIDIA Run:ai open source puts production GPU scheduling, quotas and workload management in developers’ hands. The release, makes Run:ai part of the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory platform. Platform teams can now inspect, fork and self-host the stack without a paid subscription. NVIDIA Run:ai is an AI workload and GPU orchestration platform for Kubernetes from NVIDIA. It schedules development, training and inference workloads across shared GPU clusters. It runs on top of Kubernetes and does not replace it. The control plane handles workload submission, resource management and monitoring. Cluster services run on each Kubernetes cluster and add GPU-aware scheduling. Users reach it through a web UI, CLI, REST API and an MCP server for AI assistants. NVIDIA split the release into 4 components that teams can adopt independently: The local development guide stands on 1 script, local-dev.sh . It builds about 50 Go services from source inside containers. It then creates a 5-node Kind cluster pinned to Kubernetes v1.32.5. A fake GPU operator simulates 8 Tesla-A10 GPUs, so no GPU hardware is required. The --gpu-operator flag switches to real NVIDIA GPUs. That mode needs Linux, Docker and the NVIDIA Container Toolkit. AMD and Intel accelerators are not supported. Dev teams can deploy from source or from the NGC Community Product Helm chart. That edition needs no paid subscription but excludes NVIDIA enterprise support. Teams can also adopt it through 8 DSX ecosystem partners. These are Crusoe , Mirantis , Nebius , OpenNebula Systems , Rafay , Saturn Cloud , Spectro Cloud and vCluster . Supported commercial editions continue through NVIDIA AI Enterprise, NVIDIA Mission Control and select cloud marketplaces. Two adjacent projects round out the stack. Model Streamer streams model weights directly into GPU memory. vLLM and SGLang enable it with --load-format runai_streamer . Microsoft’s published benchmark used 8 NVIDIA H100 VMs. It showed 3x to 6x faster loading than the default loader. Throughput held at 80 Gbps versus about 40 Gbps on the default path. Grove orchestrates multicomponent inference workloads. It starts components such as prefill and decode as all-or-nothing units. The key difference is scope. Volcano, Kueue and YuniKorn focus on scheduling or queueing. Run:ai ships a full management platform on top of its scheduler. Check out the GitHub repo , the local dev guide and NVIDIA’s technical blog . All credit goes to the researcher of this project. item.title: Mistral AI Releases Timestral: A 209M Forecasting Model Family That Outperforms Google’s TimesFM-3
item.abstract: Mistral AI has released Timestral , its first family of time series foundation models. Timestral is a set of 4 zero-shot forecasting models from Mistral AI, sized from 5M to 209M parameters. The largest checkpoint ranks first among pretrained, zero-shot models on GIFT-Eval, TIME and fev-bench. It does this without a GPU at inference. For developers, this Timestral time series foundation model means probabilistic forecasts on standard server CPUs, with open weights and inference code . Timestral is a time series foundation model (TSFM). It is pretrained on a large, diverse corpus, then forecasts zero-shot on data it has never seen. Classical tools like ARIMA fit one series at a time. Deep models like PatchTST usually train from scratch on each dataset. Timestral transfers patterns across domains instead. Each model outputs 21 quantiles per time step . It forecasts multivariate targets jointly. It accepts past-only, known-future and categorical covariates. Timestral is a causal, patch-based transformer with time attention and variate attention. The 209M model uses 24 layers and an embedding dimension of 768 . Each patch covers 32 time steps. A single forward pass forecasts up to 1,024 steps. Longer horizons run block by block, feeding each block’s median back as context. Mistral lists 4 technical contributions : All scores below are zero-shot, from a single checkpoint without ensembling. They come from the Timestral-209M model card . The size scaling is flat at the top. Timestral-123M scores 0.659 MASE on GIFT-Eval , against 0.658 for 209M. Mistral team states that the 28M model beats Chronos-2 on GIFT-Eval and TIME. Chronos-2 is about 4 times larger. Mistral team tested a standard server CPU with 8 threads. The task: forecast 1 day ahead from 3 weeks of 15-minute history. The 5M model took 10 ms and the 209M model took 140 ms . The 28M model is 5 times faster than 209M. The 123M model lands within 0.2% of the 209M score at three quarters of its latency. * As listed on the Timestral-209M model card . Google and Amazon do not publish matching figures on their own model pages. ** From Datadog’s model card . Mistral’s card lists 0.642 / 0.539. Install the package with pip install git+https://github.com/mistralai/timestral.git . It needs Python 3.10+ and torch 2.4+ . Dependencies are PyTorch, NumPy, safetensors and huggingface_hub. Weights download from Hugging Face: 21 MB for 5M, 111 MB for 28M, 490 MB for 123M . Mistral’s docs list Timestral 1.0 209M as Public Preview . Fine-tuning on proprietary data runs through Mistral Forge . The pipeline can deploy on-prem, in a VPC or air-gapped. Check out the blog post , GitHub repo and model weights on Hugging Face . item.title: Push-based KV transfer to improve TTFT and TPOT for disaggregated inference in vLLM
item.abstract: vLLM is an open-source inference and serving engine for large language models (LLMs). LLM inference has two distinct phases: prefill, which processes the input prompt and builds the key-value (KV) cache, and decode, which uses that cache to generate output one token at a time. These phases have different compute, memory, and scaling characteristics. Prefill-decode (P-D) disaggregation runs them on separate engine instances, allowing each phase to scale and be optimized independently. This can improve resource utilization, throughput, and latency under load. However, it also requires transferring the KV cache from the prefill instance to the decode instance before token generation can begin, making efficient KV transfer critical to time-to-first-token (TTFT). One of the ways vLLM performs this transfer is through the NVIDIA Inference Xfer Library (NIXL) connector , which moves KV blocks over interconnects that support Remote Direct Memory Access (RDMA), such as AWS Elastic Fabric Adapter ( AWS EFA , the low-latency RDMA network used across servers in AWS). On supported instance types , AWS EFA supports GPUDirect RDMA and Neuron Direct RDMA. NIXL can therefore transfer KV blocks directly between GPU or AWS Trainium device memory without staging through host memory. The default mode for NIXL connector is pull-based : After the prefill instance finishes computing the prompt KV cache, the router relays the source metadata, including the prefill block IDs, to the decode instance. The decode instance then allocates destination blocks, prepares the NIXL transfer, and initiates NIXL READ to pull the KV blocks from the prefill instance. Because these coordination and setup steps occur sequentially after prefill and before decoding can begin, they extend the TTFT critical path, as shown in the following timeline. Figure 1: Pull-mode KV transfer timeline, where the router relay, decode-side allocation, and NIXL READ run serially on the path to the first token This post introduces a push-based NIXL connector that moves post-prefill transfer coordination and setup off the critical path. If you run disaggregated prefill/decode inference with vLLM, push mode can improve application responsiveness by reducing TTFT and TPOT, particularly at high request rates. In our benchmark on a 1P1D deployment using Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) P5en instances connected with EFA, push mode delivered up to 3x better TTFT and up to 30 percent better time-per-output-token (TPOT) compared to pull mode (see the Performance data section) for the Qwen3-32B model. Results depend on workload and configuration. We built and validated the feature on AWS Trainium instance clusters connected with EFA, and then we contributed it to vLLM as an accelerator-agnostic feature. The results here are from an Amazon EC2 P5en (GPU) cluster with EFA, showing the gains carry over to GPUs. This post explains the push-based architecture, transfer flow, threading model, performance results, and how to reproduce the benchmark. This section explains the push-based design: its architecture, the transfer protocol, and the threading model that keeps KV transfer off the critical path. Push-based transfer improves TTFT and decode throughput for two reasons: The net effect is lower TTFT and higher output-token throughput on the decode instance. The push connector coordinates three actors: the decode instance registers its target blocks up front, the prefill instance matches each request and issues the transfer, and a dedicated background thread carries the KV write off the engine’s forward-pass loop. The following diagram shows how these pieces fit together. Figure 2: Push-based KV transfer architecture, showing how the decode instance, prefill instance, and background transfer thread coordinate The protocol has three logical steps. 1. Registration (decode side). When the decode instance allocates local blocks for a request requiring remote prefilling, it prepares a registration describing where the prefill instance should write the KV: its own identity and the block locations it has just reserved. Within the same engine step, the worker transmits this registration to the prefill instance as a NIXL notification. Because registration happens at allocation time, the connector knows the destination blocks before the prefill instance completes prefill. 2. Rendezvous (prefill side). The registration from the decoder and the completion of prefill on the producer can arrive in either order, and the connector handles both. If the registration arrives first, the producer holds it until its own prefill finishes. If prefill finishes first, the producer holds the request’s blocks until the registration arrives. Whichever event happens second triggers the transfer. The connector pairs requests by ID, and the matching accounts for reissued requests, correctly associating preempted or retried requests. 3. Transfer (prefill side). Once a request is matched, the producer establishes a connection to the decode instance (if one does not already exist) and issues an NIXL WRITE that copies the KV blocks directly into the decoder’s registered memory, addressing each destination tensor-parallel rank. The producer and consumer may use different internal block layouts. Each side maps block locations to its own physical layout at transfer time, allowing different block sizes on each side. Each WRITE carries a completion notification that NIXL delivers to the decode instance once the data arrives. The decoder counts these notifications, one per producer rank that writes into it. It treats the KV as received only after all expected notifications have arrived, at which point the request proceeds to decode. The push connector separates model execution from KV-transfer preparation by using a dedicated background transfer thread on each prefill worker. At the start of a request, the decode main loop allocates its destination KV blocks and registers them with the prefill instance while the prefill main loop computes the prompt KV cache. After both the destination registration and prompt KV are ready, the prefill main loop hands the KV blocks to the background thread and quickly returns to model execution. The background thread establishes or reuses the NIXL connection, maps the request’s KV block IDs to memory descriptors, merges contiguous blocks into larger transfer regions, and submits the NIXL WRITE to the decode instance. When NIXL completes the transfer, it sends a completion notification to the decode instance, which then begins token generation. Keeping descriptor preparation and transfer submission off the latency-critical main loops prevents this per-request work from delaying model execution. The following diagram shows these main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request. Figure 3: Main-loop and background-thread handoffs for a single request in the push-based threading model The following diagram summarizes the pull and push transfer flows described in the preceding sections and highlights their effect on TTFT. Although both modes use the same NIXL and EFA/RDMA data path, pull performs the metadata relay and decode-side setup after prefill, while push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill. As a result, push removes these operations from the post-prefill critical path, allowing decoding to begin sooner. Figure 4: Pull and push transfer flows compared, highlighting how push overlaps decode-side setup with prefill The two modes also involve a routing tradeoff. Pull mode allows the router to select a decode instance after prefill completes, which provides greater flexibility for load-aware routing and quality-of-service management. Push mode selects the decode instance earlier so that destination setup can overlap with prefill. In return, under comparable load, the prefill instance can release its KV blocks sooner because the transfer starts as soon as both the prompt KV and destination registration are ready.

item.title: Accelerating Mamba-2 with High-Performance Forward Pass Kernels in NVIDIA CUDA Tile
item.abstract: NVIDIA CUDA Tile (cuTile) is a Python-based DSL and parallel programming model for NVIDIA GPUs that automatically leverages advanced hardware capabilities to deliver peak performance for tile-level GPU programming. By abstracting thread- and warp-level scheduling behind high-level, tile-centric primitives, cuTile enables you to write GPU kernels in Python while compiler optimizations automatically target advanced hardware features like Tensor Cores. As an early adopter of cuTile, machine learning engineers at Jane Street implemented Mamba-2, a state-of-the-art sequence model, in cuTile and partnered with NVIDIA to optimize the kernels. Jane Street is a deeply technical global trading firm, using deep learning to drive innovation in advanced quantitative research. This post walks you through the three custom kernels powering the Mamba-2 forward pass and the cuTile optimizations behind them. Overview and prerequisites To use cuTile, ensure your environment meets the requirements outlined in the cuTile Python Quickstart guide. Import the package as cuda.tile and expose it as ct throughout the kernel implementations featured in this post. Sequence modeling computational trade-off Sequence modeling architectures face a computational trade-off: traditional softmax attention trains rapidly using matrix multiplication accelerated by Tensor Cores, but at inference, compute and memory requirements increase linearly with sequence length. In contrast, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) suffer from slow, nonparallelizable training but require constant compute and fixed memory footprint regardless of sequence length. Mamba-2 architecture The Mamba-2 architecture comes from a family of models aiming for the best of both worlds. Similar to an RNN, it has a fixed size hidden state and a recurrent update that can be computed chunkwise in a computationally efficient manner using Tensor Cores. The core recurrence of Mamba-2 is: \(h_t = \exp(A \cdot dt_t) h_{t-1} + dt_t B_t x_t\) y t = c t ⊤ h t + D x t y_t = c_t^\top h_t + D x_t Where: \(x_t\), \(dt_t\), \(B_t\), and \(c_t\) are the inputs to the Mamba-2 layer (obtained by projecting the inputs to the block, like queries, keys and values in an attention layer) at token \(t\) \(y_t\) is the output at token \(t\) \(h_t\) is the fixed-size hidden state carried across tokens. It’s not a vector as in RNNs, but a matrix (more numbers and more representational capacity) \(A\) and \(D\) are learned model parameters Intuitively: \(dt_t\) (one scalar per head) represents how much of the state should be updated. All values in \(dt\) are negative Because the previous state is multiplied \(\exp(Adt_t)\), the state stays the same when \(dt_t = 0\) \(x_t\) (a vector of size H) plays a role similar to the values in attention \(B_t\) (a vector of size S) plays a role similar to the keys in attention \(c_t\) (a vector of size S) is how the state is mixed to produce the outputs and plays a role similar to the queries in attention The state \(h_t\) is a matrix of size S,H (\(B_t x_t^\top\) is an outer product). To make computation easier to write, use \(a_t = Adt_t\) and call \(b_t\) the product \(dt_t B_t\). The equation is then simply: \(h_t = \exp(a_t)h_{t-1} + b_t x_t^{\mathsf{T}}, y_t = c_t^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t-1} + Dx_t\) This recurrent formulation is ideal for sequential inference. However, training and prefill require something faster than a for-loop. While the linear state update allows for a parallel scan algorithm, this approach requires materializing an enormous hidden state tensor making it primarily memory-bound and unable to utilize Tensor Cores. An alternative approach leverages Tensor Cores by computing any future hidden state directly through matrix multiplication. Ignoring the \(\exp(a_t)\) term for simplification, going from \(h_t\) to \(h_{t+T}\) is just: \(h_{t+T} = h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + b_{t+2}x_{t+2}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+T}x_{t+T}^{\mathsf{T}}\) If building a matrix \(B\) of shape ( T, S ) by stacking all of the \(b_{t+i}\) and a matrix \(X\) of shape ( T, H ) by stacking all of the \(x_{t+i}\) then this is just \(h_{t+T} = h_t + BX^T\): Figure 1. Update to state after a chunk of events With this jump formula, you can efficiently compute the hidden state at various chunk “checkpoints” in the sequence. The next step is to find a way to compute outputs \(y_1\), \(y_2\), \(y_3\), \(y_4\) given only \(h_0\). This would be easy if computing \(h_1\), \(h_2\), \(h_3\), \(h_4\), … but doing so would defeat the point of the jump formula. Still removing the decay term \(\exp(a_t)\) for now, the goal is to compute: \(y_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}h_{t+i} + Dx_{t+i} = c_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}}\left(h_t + b_{t+1}x_{t+1}^{\mathsf{T}} + \cdots + b_{t+i}x_{t+i}^{\mathsf{T}} \right) + Dx_{t+i}\) Where the previous formula is used to expand the hidden state. The skip connection term \(Dx_{t+i}\) is easy to reason about. For the others, it looks like this: Figure 2. Computing a chunk of outputs from one state without materializing intermediate hidden states Again, grouping a chunk of \(x_t\), \(b_t\), \(c_t\) and \(y_t\) in matrices enables re-expressing this with Tensor Core-friendly matrix products (Figure 3) where the triangle in the \(\mathit{C}\) by \(\mathit{B}\) product is a causal mask (like in causal softmax attention). When computing the output \(y_{t+i}\) you have some product of \(c_{t+i}\) by all of the \(b_j\) for \(j \leq t + i\) so when computing the full matrix product, you need to mask out the ones in the future (above the diagonal). In math this becomes (adding back the skip connection): \(Y = Ch_t + \left((CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) With \(M\) the traditional causal mask. Figure 3. Mamba-2 chunk computation Note that this looks very similar to attention (without the softmax) because when the decay term is removed, Mamba-2 is just linear attention (with some renaming). Adding back the decay makes things a little bit trickier. The expansion of the recurrence will look like: \(h_(t+T)=exp⁡(a_(t+1)+a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) h_t+exp⁡(a_(t+2)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+1) x_(t+1)+exp⁡(a_(t+3)+⋯+a_(t+T) ) b_(t+2) x_(t+2)+⋯+b_(t+T) x_(t+T)\) Reformulating in log-space allows for replacing sequential multiplications with cumulative sums. This remains a matmul if the rows of \(B\) (or \(X\)) are pre-multiplied by the exponentials. Keeping track of the cumulative sum of \(a_t\) in a tensor \(G\), this results in the following new equation: \(h_{t+T} = \exp(G_{last})h_t + \left(\exp(G_{last} – G)\cdot B\right)X^{\mathsf{T}}\) Plugging the new hidden state jump into the output computation results in the following: \(Y = \exp(G)Ch_{kT} + \left(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot (CB^{\mathsf{T}})\cdot M\right)X + DX\) where the matrix \(\exp(G – G^{\mathsf{T}})\) contains at \((i, j)\) the term \(\exp(g_i – g_j)\). Note that all of the terms where \(i < j\) will be masked by the causal mask, so only keep terms where \(g_t\) is the sum of more of the \(a_t\) than \(g_j\). By construction, all \(a_t\) values are negative, which makes \(g_i – g_j\) negative. Any exponentials of positive numbers are never kept, guaranteeing numerical stability. Figure 4. Causal masking to make the exponential safe This will translate into three kernels: chunk_cumsum : Compute the cumulative sums of the \(a_t\) inside each chunk. fwd_pass_state : Compute the hidden state at the beginning of each chunk using the jump formula above. compute_out : Compute the outputs for each chunk using the initial hidden state for the chunk computed in the previous step. Kernel 1: Computing cumulative sums The cumulative sums of the \(a_t = Adt_t\) (the \(G\) in the previous math) are needed in both Steps 2 and 3. To avoid recomputing several times, this first kernel will compute \(a_t\) once and store it. Note that this is not a global cumulative sum, just the cumulative sum within each chunk.

item.title: I Can See Everything
item.abstract: Nick Cammarata of Goodfire makes a bold claim: Neural Networks are Already Clean . This was his follow up after various resulting online discussions . This is clearly good work that tells us new and important things. The question is, how big an update is this, how much progress does it represent and what is the outlook going forward? The reactions here range from the super optimistic takes of ‘this means mechanistic interpretability is solvable,’ or even ‘all but solved,’ with comparisons to the famous paper Attention is All You Need . Dean W. Ball (OpenAI): There is so much to say about this, and I will, but WOW, congratulations to Nick and Goodfire. This may be one of the most important single days in deep learning history, and perhaps much more than that. No matter what, this is a victory for the dogged pursuit of understanding. roon (OpenAI): when nick told me that he had some interp breakthroughs, he was uh, underselling it. i think this may be remembered as a major moment in scientific history. news so good even Eliezer will have to lower his pdoom. we can start making alignment into a ‘normal science’ This paper is solid and meaningful contribution that is in some ways overstated. Get excited, but also there are those who need to take a chill pill. We did not actually get an apples-to-apples jump from 1.7% to 90% interpretability of LLM neurons. I interpret Eliezer as slightly lowering his p(doom), but not all that much . Evžen Wybitul : What’s happening? Half of my tl is non-interp people from OAI painting the post as the second coming of Christ and the other half is interp researchers (including Leo Gao) saying it’s… fine This post is my attempt to sort this out. Currently I am landing somewhere in the middle. It is an important update about how LLMs and minds form and operate. It tells us how to go about some useful tasks and reduces our estimate of some task difficulties. Great work, assuming the work checks out. The whole thing very much has a ring of truth, and of a person being curious. You love to see it. What it does not tell us is that interpretability will soon be solved, or is about to be made into a science, let alone that alignment will soon be handled. The hype got rather out of hand in some places. Table of Contents Good Smoke, Potential Fire. One Neuron, One Central Concept. I Can See Everything. What a Concept. The More You Know. Attention Is Still What You Need. Occam’s Razor. The Neurons Sometimes Share Clear Themes. Hype. Anti-Hype. Theme and Variations. Is This How Minds Work? But We Can Open The Box, Said Toad. That Was Not the Hard Problem. More Skepticism. That’s All There Is, There Ain’t No More. The Default Outcome of Mech Interp is Goodhart’s Law. Interpretability is Dual Use. Now The Work Can Begin. Good Smoke, Potential Fire Before I cover reactions or take a side, here are my highlights. It is worth reading at least this much of the primary source. Reading the whole thing is an option, but it is long and the writing can be easy to bounce off of and can repeat itself. Nick Cammarata, Goodfire : The cause of polysemanticity in early model organisms wasn’t superposition, but several ordinary, mostly fixable issues. We can now understand most neurons in models up to trillions of parameters, and think the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than we thought. I think I have good news about the nature of neural networks. After many months studying neurons and circuits in image and language models, I’ve come to believe a network’s own mechanisms are its legible building blocks, and that the outlook for mechanistic interpretability may be far better than I’d feared. The canonical evidence of polysemanticity and superposition that convinced much of the field, including me, that networks pack concepts arbitrarily was misread. What looked like arbitrary packing was mostly a motif I’ll call recursive generalization, which is much less concerning. One Neuron, One Central Concept The central claim is that for larger LLMs, most neurons represents a singular concept and things clustered around that concept, perhaps with small offshoots and some use of low-level activations. … Modern language models are also far more interpretable than generally believed. … With better tools and modern models, the situation looks quite different. In preliminary audits of Qwen3-32B, we estimate that roughly 90% of neuron poles have one main job, often with small related offshoots; another ~7% have two related jobs; and only ~2-4% are not yet understood. Dense and Mixture of Experts models seem roughly similar. We found similar results in models up to trillions of parameters, like Kimi K3, which the companion paper will cover in more detail. Where previously the working theory was that models overloaded neurons with unrelated concepts in superposition, Nick’s theory is you did not think sufficiently hard to identify the unifying concept. Each neuron is a generalization, mostly ones we can readily understand if we look. … What matters a lot more is why things share a neuron in the first place. Most of the remaining apparent polysemanticity seems to be a motif I call recursive generalization. It’s simple: as a neuron grows, it sprouts offshoots the way a tree branch sprouts sub-branches. For instance, one neuron that detected “iy” grew to detect “diy,” and then “do it yourself,” which doesn’t contain “iy” at all. … So there were two explanations for polysemanticity, and I helped propose both. In some ways, they’re opposites: generalization groups similar things together and superposition groups unrelated things together. Superposition is the one the field bet on and, until recently, so did I. But I now think recursive generalization was basically right. … Interpretability has a surprising amount of momentum: like a jigsaw puzzle or crossword, any understanding you gain starts constraining the rest of the system. … Take a neuron that tracks ‘a sense of righteousness when a bargain purchase turns out to work better than the expensive alternative’. Neurons that track a feeling or social cue like this are some of the most common we’ve found. This pictures intelligence as brute force. Neurons are compound words in German. New concept? Go get another neuron. And yet, it works. I Can See Everything … The bad news about modern neural networks is that they’re enormous. The good news is that the enormity helps: as the map fills in, every explanation is tightly constrained by everything around it, and bigger models learn narrower neurons that are easier to recognize in the first place. In this sense, understanding the whole network may be easier than understanding just the parts we care about most. Nick argues that this means that it is easier to solve the full puzzle and understand everything, and then take a measurement of your specific area of interest, then to try to directly pull a fuzzy concept like ‘deception’ out of a pool of mystery neurons. … “deception” is a useful initial frame, but the building blocks that contribute to deceptive behavior by models probably have alignment-relevant microstructure that will be hard to know without going in and looking. … All of this has brought me back to an old hope: understanding a neural network directly, by studying its mechanisms and the data flowing between them, without first trying to fix or untangle it. Put together, the argument has four steps. Networks use one learning principle, not two (if not everywhere, then nearly enough that it doesn’t matter for study), so there’s no blocker to beginning ordinary science on them. With modern models and tools, that science goes much better than most people expect. Understanding compounds, so it gets easier as the map fills in. At minimum, then, a network’s own mechanisms should be part of the toolkit.

item.title: LangChain vs. LlamaIndex vs. Building From Scratch: Here’s What I Suggest
item.abstract: LangChain vs. LlamaIndex vs. Building From Scratch: Here’s What I Suggest Choosing the right framework for your large language model application comes down to one question: what are you actually optimizing for? By Vinod Chugani on October 19, 2026 in Artificial Intelligence The tooling ecosystem around large language models (LLMs) has expanded faster than most practitioners can track. Two names dominate nearly every conversation about LLM application development: LangChain and LlamaIndex . Both promise to reduce the friction of building with LLMs. Both have large communities and active development. And both get recommended, almost reflexively, the moment someone asks how to get started. But neither one is the right answer for every team, every project, or every stage of development. A third path is increasingly worth serious consideration: building from scratch, using nothing but the base APIs and your own abstractions. This guide breaks down what each approach actually offers, where each one creates problems, and how to decide which path fits your situation. The goal isn't to crown a winner. It's to help you make a deliberate choice rather than defaulting to whatever has the most GitHub stars. Understanding What These Tools Actually Do Before comparing them, it helps to be precise about the problem they solve. LLMs on their own are stateless text predictors. They take a prompt, return a completion, and remember nothing. Building useful applications on top of them — things like document question-answering systems, multi-step agents, retrieval pipelines, or conversational interfaces — requires orchestration: managing context, routing between tools, retrieving relevant information, handling memory, and chaining operations together. LangChain and LlamaIndex both provide that orchestration layer. They abstract away the plumbing so developers can focus on application logic rather than infrastructure. Building from scratch means writing that plumbing yourself. LangChain: Broad, Flexible, Occasionally Overwhelming LangChain arrived early and built an enormous surface area. Its strength is breadth. It provides abstractions for chains, agents, memory, tools, retrievers, output parsers, prompt templates, and dozens of integrations with external services, databases, and APIs. Where It Works Well Teams that need to connect LLMs to a wide variety of external tools and data sources will find LangChain's integration library genuinely useful. It covers a remarkable range of providers — from vector databases to search engines to custom APIs — and the community has produced extensive documentation and examples for common patterns. LangChain also handles multi-step agentic workflows reasonably well. If your application needs an LLM to decide between tools, loop on results, or execute a sequence of actions based on intermediate outputs, LangChain's agent abstractions give you a starting point without requiring you to build the decision loop yourself. Where It Creates Friction The same breadth that makes LangChain appealing also makes it hard to reason about. The abstraction layers sit deep, and when something breaks, tracing the failure through multiple layers of wrapped classes is non-trivial. Many developers report that LangChain's abstractions initially accelerate development and then create drag during debugging and customization. The framework has also evolved rapidly, which means documentation can lag behind the current API, older tutorials may reference deprecated patterns, and upgrading between versions occasionally introduces breaking changes. For production systems that require stability and predictability, this churn is a real cost. LangChain works best when you're prototyping quickly, exploring what an LLM application could do, or building something where broad integration coverage matters more than tight control over implementation details. LlamaIndex: Focused, Opinionated, Purpose-Built for Retrieval LlamaIndex (formerly GPT Index) started with a narrower scope: making it easier to build retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems. That focus is still its defining characteristic. Where It Works Well If your application is primarily about retrieving information from documents and providing it as context to an LLM, LlamaIndex is exceptionally well-suited. Its data connectors, indexing strategies, and query engines are purpose-built for this use case, and the abstractions are generally more coherent as a result. LlamaIndex also provides solid tooling for more advanced RAG patterns: re-ranking, hybrid search, hierarchical retrieval, and query routing. Teams building production-grade document question-answering systems, knowledge base assistants, or enterprise search applications will find that LlamaIndex handles the edge cases that simpler retrieval pipelines miss. The framework has also invested meaningfully in evaluation tooling, which matters more than it might seem. Knowing whether your retrieval system is actually returning useful context — and knowing that before it affects users — is one of the harder problems in LLM application development. Where It Creates Friction LlamaIndex is less suited to applications that extend beyond retrieval. If you need rich agent behavior, complex tool use, or workflows that don't center on document retrieval, you may find yourself fighting the framework's assumptions rather than working with them. Like LangChain, it also carries abstraction overhead. The more the framework assumes about your architecture, the harder it becomes to deviate from those assumptions when your requirements don't fit the expected pattern. Building From Scratch: More Accessible Than It Sounds "Building from scratch" doesn't mean writing an LLM from scratch. It means calling the model provider's API directly, implementing your own retrieval logic, and building only the abstractions your specific application needs. This approach has become more accessible as the base APIs have matured. OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and other providers now offer well-documented APIs with solid client libraries. Vector database providers like Pinecone , Weaviate , and Qdrant have their own SDKs. The infrastructure exists. You're choosing to assemble it yourself rather than through a framework. Where It Works Well Building from scratch gives you complete visibility into what your system is doing at every step. There are no hidden prompt injections from framework templates, no unexpected retry logic, no abstraction layers intercepting your requests. When something behaves unexpectedly, you know exactly where to look. This control becomes especially valuable in production. Teams that have taken LLM applications through the full development lifecycle frequently report that framework constraints become more painful as requirements evolve. Custom retrieval logic, specialized context management, domain-specific prompt engineering, and performance optimization are all easier when you own the implementation. There's also a less obvious benefit: building from scratch forces clarity about what your application actually needs. Frameworks can encourage over-engineering by making complex patterns easy to reach for. When you're implementing retrieval yourself, you'll naturally implement exactly what your use case requires — no more, no less. Where It Creates Friction The upfront investment is real. You'll write more code initially, make more decisions explicitly, and spend more time on infrastructure that frameworks would handle automatically. For teams exploring whether an LLM application is viable at all, that investment may delay learning. There's also a knowledge requirement worth being honest about. Building a good RAG pipeline from scratch requires understanding embedding models, vector similarity, chunking strategies, and context window management. Frameworks can paper over knowledge gaps that scratch-built systems will expose.
