item.title: Laplace Intelligence red-teams robots and self-driving cars before they hit the real world
item.abstract: If there’s one lesson the OpenAI-Hugging Face incident taught us, it’s that AI agents can be unpredictable. “Imagine if something like that happened in the physical world,” Howie Sun, CEO and co-founder of Laplace Intelligence , told TechCrunch. “AI agents are moving from computers into the real world, and we don’t really want physical AI to fail in the real world.” Ann Arbor-based Laplace is building automated red-teaming — essentially, stress-testing a system by deliberately trying to make it fail — for robotics and physical AI. The company is betting that the only way to make sure physical AI is safe is to have AI test it. “Our goal is to help companies discover and fix problems before deployment — and, over time, build a shared foundation of evidence that customers, insurers, and regulators can trust,” Sun said. Laplace is one of 20 startups competing in Startup Battlefield 200, the startup pitch competition taking place at TechCrunch Disrupt in San Francisco this week, October 13-15. It will present on the Disrupt Stage Tuesday afternoon , October 13. Howie Sun, CEO, Laplace Intelligence. Image Credits: Laplace Intelligence Sun, alongside his co-founder and chief scientist Henry Liu, founded Laplace a year ago out of the University of Michigan. Sun has spent the last eight years in academia researching how to challenge autonomous driving AI in simulation. In 2023, he and Liu — his then-PhD adviser — published a paper on the subject that made it onto the cover of the top scientific journal Nature. That’s when the calls started coming in from autonomous vehicle companies interested in implementing their ideas. “I realized that I wanted to build this and take it from purely academic research into a product that’s useful in the real world,” Sun said. Using their academic research as a base, Sun and Liu built Laplace, so named for “Laplace’s demon,” an 1814 thought experiment by French scholar Pierre-Simon Laplace, who imagined that if you knew the exact state of everything in the universe, you could predict the future with total precision. “We are essentially using simulation to predict the real world’s future,” Sun said. At the startup’s core is a high-fidelity simulation reconstructed from the real world, paired with an AI agent that constantly probes for weaknesses and failure points. The goal is to ensure that any physical AI — be it a robot, autonomous vehicle, or smart city solution — is safe in simulation before it’s deployed in the real world. The simulation environment is a post-trained version of Nvidia’s Cosmos, an AI world simulation platform, which is grounded in the real world, allowing Laplace to reconstruct anything from an Arizona highway to a Paris pedestrian crossing. Simulations are generated by blending a mesh of different real-world information. A Google Street View image could serve as a reference from which an entire street is generated. But rather than generating something random, the simulator combines real-world map data to re-create an environment that’s true to scale. Developers can then use language prompts to change the setting in real time, like adding in afternoon traffic. Sun says Laplace pulls real-time traffic and congestion information from navigation providers like TomTom. Within Laplace’s simulations, not only is the environment simulated, but also the behavior of other actors. For example, during a demo, Sun directed the test agent vehicle to swerve into oncoming traffic. The car it would have hit — or driven through, as is common among some generative world models — moved out of its way to avoid a collision. “It’s truly an interactive simulation environment,” Sun said. “Everyone is reacting to everything … This is more like a world model with interactive participants.” While the simulated environment is an important part of Laplace’s product, the real unique selling point is the AI agents the startup is developing to automatically design corner cases (tricky, rare scenarios that could trip up an AI system), moving the human further out of the loop. “They can design from the news, from police reports on collisions — all kinds of information to actively challenge the autonomous vehicles and other physical AI agents,” Sun said. Henry Liu, chief scientist, Laplace Intelligence. Image Credits: Laplace Intelligence Today, autonomous vehicle developers mostly train an AI to handle edge cases using recorded footage that they then turn into a simulation, or by relying on humans to come up with new ideas and design them. While many AV companies have done what Laplace is pitching and started embracing AI to create edge cases for training — self-driving truck company Waabi comes to mind — the need for this kind of technology will really become apparent when we start placing generalized robots in the real world. “There’s less data on generalized robotics,” Sun said. “No one knows what the edge cases will be in the real world.” Despite Sun and Liu coming from academia, with no shiny Silicon Valley tech company pedigrees, the two have managed to start generating revenue and even turn a modest profit. Most of the money is coming from autonomous driving use cases, with customers including Texas-based autonomous trucking firm Bot Auto and a major Japanese automotive manufacturer. Laplace is also working with Nvidia and T-Mobile on a free smart city pilot for San Jose, California, to provide high-level traffic operations. Laplace is also in the early stages of working with partners building humanoid robotics for warehouses. Most of Laplace’s customer contracts are project-based today, and the company is working toward turning that into recurring revenue. The startup’s near-term goal — which it hopes will be aided by competing at Disrupt — is to raise funds and scale so it can compete with its rivals. Chief among its rivals is Applied Intuition , a buzzy late-stage startup that’s raised $1.2 billion to date at a $15 billion post-money valuation. Sun isn’t too worried. He believes Laplace’s core methodology of using AI to test AI is a “new paradigm that changes the testing of physical AI entirely,” turning it into a “dynamic interactive testing process.” “That will be the biggest moat,” he said. This article has been updated to clarify Laplace’s relationship with Nvidia.

item.title: Together Post-Training: frontier-grade model shaping, the way that fits you
item.abstract: We are introducing Together Post-Training, a new service for building custom models on our platform — both from environment rewards via RL and supervision data via SFT. This service is designed to give you flexible and efficient model shaping without the heavy infra burden. Together Post-Training makes it easy to define the training loop, while we co-optimize the systems and infrastructure underneath for model quality and training speed. Nothing now stands between you and the best model that is uniquely yours . The value of custom models In 2026, training custom models for your AI workloads is no longer a niche topic. Companies are actively exploring it to reduce costs and improve task-specific performance. Instead of fixing model behaviors and improving their efficiency via context or harness engineering, many AI-native and AI-forward organizations are training specialist agents, matching the quality of frontier models at a fraction of the cost and runtime. On top of that, training the model yourself yields greater ownership and flexibility: the resulting checkpoint can be deployed in any location, further refined, or even used locally. At Together, we want to empower every AI developer with the ability to get the best model for their task, as conveniently as possible. Post-training a great model requires many iterations on data curation, training algorithms, and evaluation protocols. On top of that, infrastructure for RL is getting ever more complex, with a fine line between “an efficiency optimization” and “a silent bug that holds back your runs”. Doing so for large models reliably and at scale presents its own set of challenges. Frontier labs have entire teams solving each of the above problems. Since tackling all challenges at once is a big investment, many companies that could benefit from post-training never start it, or start and stall. Together Post-Training handles all optimizations and infrastructure without getting in the way, and our forward-deployed team partners with our customers to help with the end-to-end workflow. This lets every researcher or domain expert focus on what they do best while we take care of the rest. Together Post-Training at a glance As the complexity of post-training continues to evolve, so should the tooling around it. Together Post-Training provides a set of common abstractions familiar to ML developers, as well as control over the resources used by each experiment, while making sure that all computations under the hood are fast, cost-efficient, and, most importantly, correct. We built our service to offer the highest degree of flexibility for your experiments. You can run LoRA training, including multiple LoRA adapters sharing the same GPU capacity, as well as full-weight experiments for select models. In contrast to our fine-tuning service , the entire training loop of Together Post-Training is yours to define. You can use any data, environments, or agentic harnesses that suit your setup best, and add any steps you need (such as logging or external benchmarking) throughout the training process. The entire workflow is as follows: A high-level summary of using Together Post-Training. Left: commands executed on the user side, right: service components running on Together’s side. All experiments run on Model Resources — GPU allocations that are fully yours, not competing with others’ requests for priority. Each Model Resource can hold one or several Training Sessions, where each one corresponds to a single experiment using the same base model (for example, one set of LoRA adapters). This means you get the best rollout and training performance, as you never have to compete with other users’ requests executing on the same hardware. At the same time, dedicated GPU allocations mean you can run full-weight finetuning, going beyond LoRA when adapting to large knowledge-intensive tasks. Once you allocate the model resource and start the session, you can execute each step of the training loop. Each session contains a Trainer instance responsible for running forward/backward steps and updating the weights, as well as Generator instances for executing rollouts from the policy. For every model, we heavily optimize training and rollout performance, making sure all operations are fast and numerically aligned across stacks. In the case of SFT, you can start a model resource with 0 generators to save costs. You decide the point at which the trainer parameters are sent to the generator; we also support asynchronous RL for high GPU utilization of both components at all times, especially with long agentic rollouts. While we support a number of standard losses (from cross-entropy and GRPO to CISPO and DPPO), we also allow computing a custom training objective locally and sending its gradients to the Trainer for computing the updates. Example of training with a custom loss from Together Post-Training docs Together Post-Training launches with a range of leading open-weight models, including Muse Spark Open, GLM 5.3, Kimi K3, and Qwen 3.8-27B. We will expand the selection in the coming weeks, making sure you can use both the highest-capability frontier LLMs and efficient smaller models. Quality, performance, and efficiency Delegating the internals of post-training infrastructure can be a daunting decision. Our team has first-hand experience catching silent bugs in complex machine learning systems, from pushing the frontier of RL research to training LLMs that have served millions of users. We understand that the best training stack is the one that gets you the best model , and building such infrastructure demands careful implementation and co-design across all components. For these reasons, we prioritized quality of output models as our north star in the development of the service. One notorious example of issues affecting RL results is the alignment between training and inference engines: if the same model weights produce slightly different outputs due to mismatching numerics, the whole run might underperform or even collapse. We eliminate numerous sources of policy drift across training and inference, using both standard techniques like Rollout Routing Replay and advanced optimizations driven by our research in training stability. Beyond model quality, we also work to make each run as fast and as efficient as possible, because post-training requires multiple iterations: the sooner a run finishes and the less it costs, the more ideas you get to test. Most of the time in RL is spent on generating rollouts, which allows us to capitalize on years of research and engineering behind Together’s inference products. Our rollout engines draw on the same optimizations as our serving stack. For multi-turn agents, intelligent caching and routing minimize redundant computations while keeping memory costs bounded. On the training side, optimized parallelism and sequence packing speed up both SFT and RL steps. With Together Post-Training, you size each experiment to what it needs and do not pay more. If your experiment is bottlenecked by rollout concurrency, you can request the exact number of sampler replicas. Several LoRA experiments can share one model resource, so running a sweep doesn’t mean reserving more GPUs for every setup. We bill every model resource per GPU-minute, yet thanks to many optimizations of our dedicated and multi-LoRA serving stacks, the overall costs of training drop below token-based pricing as soon as you scale up the experiments. Optimized deployment after training When the post-training experiments are finished, it might be important to run each resulting model side by side to compare their outputs. We now support multi-LoRA adapter serving in Dedicated Model Inference: instead of starting a separate production deployment for each run, you can swap the adapters at your convenience in a single GPU deployment, helping you lower the serving costs.

item.title: Superlite: A Faster Alternatie to Superpowers
item.abstract:
One at a time, versus all at once Animation. In the top lane, a single agent builds six blocks one after another while a person waits, a question bubble pops up between every block, and a clock spins. In the bottom lane, six agents build all six blocks at once, a big check mark appears in under half the time, and the person gets a cup of coffee. ? one at a time all at once I had a dream. I would hand an agent a spec, close the laptop, make a sandwich, and come back to finished, tested, committed work. Here's what actually happened. I handed over the spec. I made the sandwich. I came back. The agent had written one paragraph and was asking, very politely, whether I approved section 1 of the design. I approved it. I sat down. I waited. Section 2. Approve? Yes. Section 3. Approve? Yes. The spec? Yes. The plan? Yes, obviously, it's the plan I just watched you write. And how would I like the plan executed? However is fastest, please, I beg you. Then it started building. One task. Then a review of that task. Then a fix for the review. Then a re-review of the fix. Then the next task. I watched a progress log scroll past like a train at a level crossing: no stopping it, no getting past it, and no idea how many carriages were left. I'd refresh the terminal. Still on task 3. I'd answer an email. Still on task 3. I'd start a second sandwich purely to have something to do with my hands. Task 4, under review. The sandwiches were very good. The software didn't exist yet. And the worst part wasn't the time. It was that I couldn't leave. Every time I walked away, I came back to a question that had been sitting there for twenty minutes, waiting for me to type "yes." I didn't want a collaborator that needed me every four minutes. I wanted a contractor. Here's the spec, here's the key, call me when it's done. So I built superlite : a Claude Code plugin that plans a build, splits it into tasks that can run side by side, hands each one to the cheapest agent that can do it well, checks the seams between them, and reviews the result. Then it leaves you a tidy list of every decision it made while you were busy with the sandwich. This post covers why it exists, how it works, and how to use it. The benchmarks are there to show I'm not just saying it's fast because I wrote it. Why I built it First, a disclaimer, because I like this project and don't want angry emails. I use superpowers a lot. It's a careful, collaborative workflow that keeps a human close to every step, and it's genuinely excellent at that. Superlite borrows its bones shamelessly: the plugin layout, the session-start hook, the lifecycle skills. Credit where it's due, and then some. But when I already knew exactly what I wanted, most of the time went on the workflow waiting for itself. I profiled it, the way you'd check your bank statement after a suspicious weekend. The time went to five places: 8–12 human gates per feature. One question per message, designs approved section by section, then separate reviews of the spec, the plan, and the method of executing the plan. It's very thorough. It's also how a four-hour meeting gets scheduled. Strictly sequential execution. One implementer, then one reviewer, then the next task. On my first benchmark that was a single-file queue of 21 dispatches, like a bank with one teller and a very long lunch. A review after every task, with re-review loops. About 12 minutes of a 34-minute build. The full test suite, re-run by several skills. In case it changed its mind. Opus subagents on the critical path, writing code at about half Sonnet's speed. Brilliant, thoughtful, and in no hurry whatsoever. None of these are mistakes. Each one is a sensible safety net. Stacked together, they're perfect when you want to steer every step, and slightly maddening when you just want the thing built. So superlite isn't a rival to superpowers. It's tuned for a different job: autonomous development, at speed. If you want to steer each step, use superpowers. If you want to hand over a spec and come back to working code, use superlite . Just don't enable both in the same session. They share skill names, both inject context at startup, and they argue like siblings in the back seat. How it works The short version: one approval, a plan written for parallelism, agents matched to the work, and rules enforced by code because, as it turns out, agents read the rules and then do what they like. flowchart LR A([Your request]) --> B[One batch of questions] B --> C[Plan] C --> D[Agents build
in parallel] D --> E[Review and fix] E --> F([Done]) One batch of questions, one approval. Superlite sizes the request first. A typo just gets fixed, without a design document about the typo. A change to an existing flow gets a short design in chat. A new project gets one batch of up to four questions, then one design-and-plan document. You approve it once. After that it only stops for things that are destructive, outward-facing or security-sensitive. It won't push to main while you're getting lunch. It will do everything else. You choose who's in charge. With a human orchestrator, you see the whole plan with its predicted schedule and approve it before anything runs. With an AI orchestrator, you're not needed at all, which is either freeing or mildly insulting depending on your mood. Every choice it would normally ask about gets recorded as a ruling: what it decided, why, and what it costs if it got that wrong. When you come back, you know exactly which decisions to second-guess first. A plan written for the split. The plan is a task graph. Each task lists the files it owns, the exact interfaces it consumes and produces, and the tests it has to pass. Tasks that don't share files and don't depend on each other run at the same time. The graph decides how wide the build goes. On the current benchmark that peaked at 18 agents working at once, which is roughly the size of a small startup, minus the ping-pong table. Agents matched to the work. The org chart: Opus coordinates. It plans and dispatches, and it is not allowed to touch the code. Management, basically. Sonnet builds most of the tasks. Haiku builds only small, fully specified "mechanical" tasks that aren't on the critical path. The intern gets the well-defined stuff. Sonnet reviews the packages. A fresh Opus final reviewer reads a review packet built from the run's logs and returns findings only. It's never allowed to fix anything. It just points. Fix-only agents in three tiers take those findings, routed by how well the cause is understood. Gated by code, not by prompts. I learned this one the hard way. You can write "the coordinator never edits code" in a prompt in bold, in capitals, with feeling. The coordinator will read it, nod, and edit the code. So now hooks enforce it. One hook blocks the coordinator from editing project code. Another catches any raw pytest or npm test it runs and quietly turns it into a background run, so tests never block it. Another refuses to let anyone kill processes by name (there's a story there, and it's in the deep dive). A plan has to pass lint --stable before work starts, and stable tasks are sent off the moment it passes. Every run is measured. Hooks record each agent's tokens, cost and time. That feeds the next run's predictions and a soft budget that taps you on the shoulder at 70% of the cap. How to use it You'll need Claude Code, git, Python 3.10 or newer (for superlite's own tools; the project you build can be in any language), and bash (Git Bash on Windows). The source is iha2/superlite on GitHub. Install it from the marketplace: /plugin marketplace add iha2/superlite /plugin install superlite@superlite-dev Or clone iha2/superlite and load a local checkout for one session: claude --plugin-dir To check it's working, open a fresh session and send Let's make a react todo list . A working install starts brainstorming before it writes any code. (142 points, 65 comments on Hacker News)

item.title: Hackers hit AI coding tool OpenCode, running up charges on users’ AI accounts
item.abstract: OpenCode , an open-source AI coding agent that has been gaining ground among developers as an alternative to Claude Code and Cursor, said Saturday that attackers broke into an older system overnight, affecting 1.4% of users of its online platform, OpenCode Console, where some users store the API keys, or digital passwords, they use to access AI services. As the OpenCode team struggled to keep pace with the attack, the scramble to respond highlighted a growing problem: companies without vetted access to AI models with fewer safety restrictions have a hard time defending against large-scale, AI-driven cyberattacks. “We had a security breach last night related to a large-scale distillation attack that impacted 1.4% of OpenCode Console users,” the company wrote on X. “We have notified them all this morning via email.” Users who did not receive an email were not impacted, the company said. While the company didn’t specify how the distillation attack occurred, leaked API keys can help users in countries with restricted access to American models generate the high volume of outputs needed for that process. Some skeptics called the framing an overstretch, arguing that the incident was a straightforward breach whose use for distillation remains unproven. Overnight, developers began posting spending alerts and unauthorized charges on Reddit and X. “ I saw my Open AI, Anthropic, and Google AI spend alerts all fire off before going to bed wondering what was going on ,” a developer wrote . Other users reported charges in the hundreds of dollars on individual accounts; a few described totals above $1,000. Anthropic and Google both blocked the API keys they believed were exposed, while OpenAI said it worked with OpenCode to restore access and refund its API customers for credits used in the attack. OpenCode said refunds for unauthorized charges are underway. The exposed keys were confined to Console, where some users had them in workspaces. The open-source app and command-line tool were not affected, according to co-founder Dax Raad. “Note this is the OpenCode Console, not OpenCode itself, those keys never come to us,” he wrote on X. Even as users and AI companies moved to disable the exposed keys, the OpenCode team was still under pressure. Raad said attackers had been trying to break into its systems nonstop for 48 hours, requiring the team to keep AI defensive agents running around the clock. AI models that the OpenCode team turned to for analysis helped for a while, but started refusing to work when the malicious code they were asked to examine activated safety filters. “[T]hat was a bit frustrating,” he wrote on X. OpenCode later received access to OpenAI’s Daybreak Blue program, which gives vetted users AI models that are less likely to refuse requests for defensive security work. Raad said the access improved the team’s ability to investigate the attack. OpenCode isn’t the first company to hit this wall. In July, AI platform Hugging Face said commercial AI models blocked its attempts to analyze activity logs from an intrusion by autonomous AI agents, which OpenAI later revealed were its own models running with safeguards lowered during a test. In a section of its blog post titled “The asymmetry problem,” Hugging Face wrote that guardrails “cannot distinguish an incident responder from an attacker.” Security researchers have raised similar complaints , saying the restrictions are inconsistent and have pushed some toward foreign open-weight models, which anyone can download and run. The weekend episode drew a response from David Sacks, co-chair of the President’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology. “OpenCode (and earlier Hugging Face) hit the same wall mid-attack: frontier models refused to analyze the very exploits needed for defense because the payloads tripped safety filters. The guardrails backfired,” he wrote on X . The breach occurred the same night OpenCode made GLM-5.3-Flash free for users. The broader GLM-5.3 family has drawn attention from researchers who study open-weight models and note that its cybersecurity capabilities approached levels previously associated with restricted-access models like Anthropic’s Claude Mythos Preview. OpenCode has not detailed how attackers gained access to the older system, how keys were stored, or the full extent of any misuse. It has told affected users to revoke and replace their keys directly with each provider. The company said the incident remains ongoing . The breach lands amid a run of AI-enabled cyber incidents. Earlier this month, cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike said a China-based hacker likely used an AI penetration-testing agent, which probes computer systems for weaknesses, and Claude in attacks on South Korean banks . Last week, India’s cybersecurity agency warned that AI agents, including some being tested by AI companies, had reached Indian organizations’ systems without authorization.

item.title: People are using AI to make their smart TVs dumb again
item.abstract: The latest use case for AI? Dumbing down your smart TV to get rid of the bloat. A number of developers and vibe coders have recently been sharing solutions for “vibe-coding” your TV to get rid of sponsored ads, speed up the app launcher, redesign the home screen, disable tracking features, and more. One such solution, called “dumbtv,” describes its mission on its GitHub page thus: “Your TV should do what you paid for: your apps, your HDMI inputs, and nothing else. No ads from the TV itself, no watch tracking, no update you did not ask for.” Another, “ cleanyourtv ,” promises to strip the bloatware from any Android TV or Google TV over Wi-Fi, to replace the launcher with one that resembles Apple TV. While hacking consumer electronics devices to gain more control over their systems is hardly a new idea, the latest advances in AI technology have made such efforts much more accessible to anyone. With smart TVs in particular, the hacks come at a time when people have grown frustrated with being forced to watch ads and put up with their devices surveilling their viewing habits. Modern smart TVs ship with a technology called automatic content recognition (ACR), which identifies what’s playing on the screen using screenshots, audio clips, or other forms of digital fingerprinting. If these “dumb TV” hacks become more popular among everyday consumers, they have the potential to disrupt the smart TV ad industry, which profits from selling viewing data to advertisers or using it to display personalized ads on their own interfaces. As the creator of cleanyourtv, Gathin T., puts it, the idea to clean up the smart TV interface started one afternoon when he got tired of seeing the ads on his parents’ TV set. Vibe coded my parents' TV this afternoon! It was showing a sponsored ad before you could even get to Netflix. Gave Claude Code the model number, it found the TV on wifi, removed 25 Xiaomi packages and wrote a new launcher. Looks like an Apple TV now lol pic.twitter.com/E5Q4A1b0yI — Gathin (Ø,G) (@gathint) October 17, 2026 “I had Claude Code clean it up over Wi-Fi and build a simple home screen with just their apps on it. I put the prompt on GitHub, tweeted the before and after, and a few thousand people did the same to their own TVs over the next two days. Xiaomi, TCL, Sony, Fire TV, LG, a projector or two,” the developer wrote on a website for donations, linked from the project’s homepage . The solution doesn’t require gaining root access to the TV, nor does it make it impossible to return to the factory default state, if desired. Meanwhile, the dumbtv solution has been tested end-to-end on a Fire TV Edition television set and Android/Google TV platforms on TVs from Sony, TCL, Philips, Hisense, Xiaomi, and Shield. To use this hack, the developer, Muzzammil Yasin Sabuwala, suggests pointing your preferred AI agent at the dumbtv repository on GitHub. Sabuwala said he was motivated to work on dumbtv because he was tired of the ads and not being able to delve directly into the content he wanted to watch. His solution was coded using a combination of Deepseek V4.1 Flash, Claude Opus 5.5, and Claude Sonnet 5.5, he told TechCrunch, and he plans to maintain the GitHub, adding support for more models over time. introducing dumbtv – no spying – no ads from tv – fully customisable to setup just point your agent to this repo – https://t.co/prQLD17Wa4 https://t.co/z41SWJZVXt pic.twitter.com/c6R8EhljiA — Muzzammil (@DevMuzzammil) October 18, 2026 Fair warning: All these solutions are works in progress, and various users are now testing them across different TV platforms and suggesting updates and fixes. However, individuals don’t need to borrow someone else’s work from GitHub to get the job done. In one newly viral X post, Ryan Doyle explains that he simply sent Claude Code the listing for his TV and asked “Can you hack this?” The agent then talked him through the process, allowing him to remove the ads and bloatware from the TV set, speed up the lagging user interface, and customize his screensaver, he claims. Doyle then goes on to demonstrate in a video how fast and responsive the new interface is after the AI made the requested changes. This is how fast the TV moves now that Claude deleted all the BS laggy bloatware it comes with https://t.co/nUCEjqPwAO pic.twitter.com/g07CEgC1GJ — Ryan Doyle (@doooyle) October 17, 2026 Seeing posts about people “vibe-coding their TVs,” inspired one X user, Mihir Gupta, to try it himself. “One afternoon with Claude Code: 25 bloat apps disabled, the 192 MB stock launcher replaced with a custom 83 MB one, plus rotating wallpapers,” he wrote . The end result of these hacks may be mixed, however. Some people have found that Claude wouldn’t respond to their simple suggestions to “hack my TV,” necessitating more complex prompts. Others warned that AI agents could make mistakes, possibly disabling important packages or breaking things in the process. One person even said they bricked their Android TV using Claude , and another got stuck halfway through hacking their Fire TV. For those wary of using AI to fully hack their TVs, there are existing solutions for customizing Android-based smart TVs, such as home screen replacement apps ATV Launcher, Projectivy Launcher, and FLauncher.
